candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Free-will skepticism rejects basic-desert responsibility while preserving causal and attributive responsibility and forward-looking moral engagement.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly yields to Gregg, and the uninterrupted first-person explanation states the skeptical position associated with his work.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction identifies exactly which form of responsibility skepticism denies and which responsibility practices remain available without desert.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's suggestion that free-will skepticism discards responsibility as a whole.

candidates.contextSummary: After Dennett dismisses metaphysical free will, Caruso narrows his skepticism to basic desert and preserves responsibility grounded in moral formation, reconciliation, and safety.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: The core dispute is whether a desert system should be preserved when free will is defined as the control required for basic-desert responsibility.
candidates.attributionBasis: The same uninterrupted Caruso turn explicitly contrasts his position with Dan's consequentialist defense and defines his own use of free will.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This move fixes the debate's central conception of free will and directly challenges whether backward-looking desert should survive at all.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's consequentialist justification for retaining desert-based responsibility practices.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso marks broad agreement on forward-looking practices, then locates disagreement in desert, defines the relevant freedom, and questions preserving desert within Dennett's system.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Basic moral desert is a misleading construct, while sufficient ordinary moral responsibility can justify coercion, imprisonment, fines, and reputational consequences.
candidates.attributionBasis: Caruso directly invites Dan to respond, after which Dennett rejects basic desert and develops the Donald Trump coercion example in his characteristic first person.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Dennett rejects Caruso's framing and asserts that practical responsibility sufficient for legal and social sanctions does not require ultimate desert.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Caruso's claim that preserving a system of basic desert requires separate justification.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett calls basic desert a red herring and uses an unreformed offender to argue that the state may impose serious consequences on a sufficiently responsible agent.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Coercion and liberty restriction can be justified by self-defense, public safety, and least-restrictive means without invoking free will, retribution, or basic desert.
candidates.attributionBasis: The turn answers Dennett's challenge in the first person and develops Caruso's recognizable public-health quarantine model and least-restriction principle.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The quarantine model supplies the skeptic's central alternative foundation for state coercion and rebuts the claim that desert is needed for public protection.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's contention that rejecting basic desert leaves inadequate grounds for coercing serious offenders.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso accepts state coercion but grounds it in protection rather than punishment, applying the quarantine analogy to officeholding restrictions and less-punitive criminal responses.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Deterministically produced differences in reasons, character, and action do not justify differential praise, blame, punishment, or reward on basic-desert grounds.
candidates.attributionBasis: Caruso introduces the named Maya and Marina thought experiment and explicitly identifies his skeptical, source-incompatibilist conclusion within one sustained turn.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The paired deterministic-universe case directly argues that agents are not the ultimate sources needed for desert even when their actions and characters differ.
candidates.contextSummary: Caruso contrasts a robber and charitable donor in deterministic universes, removes forward-looking benefits, and argues that neither is an appropriate source for basic desert.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: Deterministic causation does not eliminate control because autonomous agents become largely self-made through sustained learning, reflection, practice, and moral education.
candidates.attributionBasis: Dennett directly addresses Gregg by name, diagnoses a confusion between causation and control, and answers the Maya and Marina thought experiment.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the principal compatibilist reply to source incompatibilism: responsibility rests on developed self-control rather than impossible absolute self-creation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Caruso's argument that deterministic histories prevent Maya and Marina from being responsible sources.

candidates.contextSummary: Dennett says the thought experiment omits upbringing and self-control, then grounds responsibility in agents' long development and allows punishment of an autonomous wrongdoer.

candidates.speaker: Daniel Dennett
candidates.proposition: An undamaged, informed, reasons-responsive, self-controlled person can meaningfully be said to have been able to do otherwise despite determinism.
candidates.attributionBasis: Following the question about alternative possibilities, Dennett gives a first-person clarification centered on degrees of freedom, self-control, and reasons-responsive functioning.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move supplies a naturalistic compatibilist interpretation of alternative possibilities and connects responsibility to ordinary capacities rather than metaphysical branching.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The challenge that the example assumes the offender genuinely could have acted otherwise.

candidates.contextSummary: After abnormal brain conditions are distinguished, Dennett explains ordinary ability to do otherwise through freedom from restraint, damage, deception, and impaired rational control.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Reasons-responsiveness and other compatibilist distinctions matter for rehabilitation and proportionate sanctions but do not by themselves ground desert-based blame or punishment.
candidates.attributionBasis: Caruso explicitly identifies what skeptics concede, names compatibilist distinctions, and contrasts their practical relevance with the disputed desert justification.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This concession isolates the precise inferential dispute: skeptics accept differences in agency while denying that those differences establish basic-desert responsibility.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's use of reasons-responsiveness and self-control to distinguish responsible from impaired agents.

candidates.contextSummary: Following examples of severely impaired offenders, Caruso accepts the distinction between responsive and unresponsive agency but assigns it forward-looking rather than desert-based significance.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: Compatibilist agent control and freedom from intentional external manipulation are distinct, and possessing agent control leaves open whether basic-desert responsibility is justified.
candidates.attributionBasis: Caruso announces a return to Dennett's causation-control distinction and develops the two loci of control before stating the unresolved sufficiency challenge.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument targets a central compatibilist premise by denying that internal reasons-responsive control alone settles responsibility under manipulation, luck, or determinism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's distinction between causation and control as a sufficient answer to skeptical challenges.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso separates internal agent control from an external manipulator's control, accuses Dennett of privileging the latter threat, and invokes several incompatibilist arguments against sufficiency.

candidates.speaker: Gregg Caruso
candidates.proposition: A malfunctioning brain implant can generate conduct while leaving compatibilist psychological conditions intact, challenging accounts that require an intentional external manipulator to undermine responsibility.
candidates.attributionBasis: Caruso refers to the book's treatment of manipulation and introduces his own malfunctioning-implant case as a counterexample to Dennett's stated response.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The case tests whether compatibilist control conditions are sufficient by presenting nonintentional causal determination that appears responsibility-undermining despite reasons responsiveness.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Dennett's response that manipulation cases threaten responsibility because external agents intentionally control the person.

candidates.contextSummary: Caruso describes Elizabeth's therapeutic implant malfunction, an induced egoistic desire, and her continued satisfaction of compatibilist conditions despite no intentional manipulating agent.
